metadata.file_name: 12. Gomez-Talal et al. (2025). Interpretable Machine Learning Models for PISA Results in Mathematics.pdf
metadata.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Models for PISA Results in Mathematics

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Spain and applies a preprocessing pipeline that first removes rows with excessive missingness (students with nine or more missing values across columns are excluded). The remaining missing values are replaced using the mean value computed over the dataset. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the ML training/evaluation stage, and it does not name any weight variables. Because the analysis is based on standard ML classifiers (e.g., SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) and the paper focuses on predictive discrimination and SHAP interpretability, the weighting strategy is not documented; readers should treat the results as model-based patterns rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is constructed by categorizing students into Low/Medium/High mathematics proficiency levels, but the paper does not explicitly state whether the categorization is derived from PISA mathematics plausible values (PV-based achievement) or from another scaled score. Because PV generation and PV-combining rules are not described, the PV handling strategy cannot be verified. This is a reporting gap given that PISA achievement is typically PV-based and PV handling affects uncertainty estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 microdata for Spain (raw dataset: 30,800 students). Excluded student rows with excessive missingness: any row with nine or more missing values across columns was removed (cutoff shown via a histogram with a 95% confidence threshold). After this exclusion, remaining missing values were imputed by replacing them with the mean value of the entire dataset. The analytic dataset was then used to create a three-category mathematics proficiency target (Low/Medium/High) and to train binary classifiers for three pairwise scenarios (Low vs High, Medium vs High, Low vs Medium).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics (Spain) — Low vs High proficiency classification
main_findings.performance_metrics: Meta-model (stacking) — AUC: 0.9766; metrics reported across Accuracy, Recall, Precision, Specificity, F1; exact values per metric not fully enumerated in the provided text.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for Spain, the study leveraged grade repetition, digital devices with screens, extra mathematics classes, number of books at home, and gender to predict mathematics proficiency (Low vs High), finding that the stacking meta-model outperformed individual classifiers with an AUC of 0.9766. This indicates that targeting grade repeaters and optimizing home learning resources (digital access and books) alongside structured extra mathematics support may improve the identification and support of students at risk of low mathematics achievement, though the results are predictive and SHAP-based interpretability does not establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics (Spain) — Medium vs High proficiency classification
main_findings.performance_metrics: Meta-model — reported as outperforming individual models across Accuracy, Recall, Precision, Specificity, F1, and AUC; exact AUC/ACC values not fully enumerated in the provided text.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for Spain, the study leveraged digital devices with screens, gender, study/homework before class, grade repetition, and extra mathematics classes to predict mathematics proficiency (Medium vs High), finding that the stacking meta-model achieved superior discrimination across the reported classification metrics. This indicates that strengthening study habits before class and ensuring effective use of digital resources may help move students from medium to high mathematics performance, though the paper’s interpretability relies on SHAP and the analysis does not document PV handling or survey-weighted estimation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics (Spain) — Low vs Medium proficiency classification
main_findings.performance_metrics: Meta-model — reported as improving ACC and generalization performance; exact metric values not fully enumerated in the provided text.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for Spain, the study leveraged grade repetition, digital devices with screens, extra mathematics classes, number of books at home, and study/homework before class to predict mathematics proficiency (Low vs Medium), finding that the ensemble meta-model provided the best overall discrimination and that SHAP highlighted grade repetition as strongly associated with low performance. This indicates that early intervention for students who repeat grades, combined with home-resource and homework-support strategies, may reduce the probability of remaining in low mathematics proficiency bands, while causality cannot be inferred from SHAP feature importance alone.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Spain (30,800 raw students; 29,282 retained after excluding rows with nine or more missing values and imputing remaining missing values with dataset means). It constructs a three-category mathematics proficiency target (Low/Medium/High) and trains eight binary classifiers (Logistic Regression, SVM, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, MLP, LightGBM) using stratified 5-fold cross-validation with random undersampling for class imbalance, then combines the best base models via a stacking meta-model with Logistic Regression as the meta-learner. The meta-model is reported to outperform individual models across Accuracy, Recall, Precision, Specificity, F1, and AUC; for Low vs High it achieves AUC = 0.9766. Interpretability is provided using SHAP (including Tree/Kernel/Linear SHAP concepts), and the dashboard links UMAP embeddings to SHAP explanations. Limitations include lack of documented PV handling and survey-weight application, and SHAP-based explanations are not causal evidence.
